name: Stream processing
summary: Queries that never finish: they read events as they arrive and keep results, counts and joins up to date.
howItWorks: A stream processor runs a query that never ends: it reads events from a stream, such as a Kafka topic, and emits results while new events keep arriving. Stateless steps, like filtering or reshaping, look at one event at a time. Stateful steps remember things between events: a join holds events until their match arrives, and an aggregation keeps a running count per key. Aggregations are cut into windows: tumbling (back-to-back minutes), hopping (overlapping, say five minutes long and starting every minute) or session (closed after a quiet gap). Windows usually follow event time, when something happened, rather than processing time, when it arrived, and a watermark says how far event time has got, so the processor knows when a window is complete. The work is split by key across parallel tasks, each keeping its state locally, in memory or in RocksDB. The processor saves that state together with its input positions (Flink in periodic checkpoints, Kafka Streams in changelog topics), so after a crash it resumes without losing or double-counting events. Exactly-once output also needs a sink that takes part, through transactions or idempotent writes.
analogy: A tally clerk at a stadium’s gates. Instead of counting everyone from the CCTV recording the next morning, they keep a running count per gate on a clipboard, call out a total every fifteen minutes, and photocopy the clipboard now and then so a stand-in can carry on from that point if they leave.
useWhen: Live metrics, counters and dashboards that have to be seconds old, not hours
Fraud, anomaly and alerting rules over a window of recent events per key
Joining or enriching one stream with another, or with a table kept current by change data capture
Streaming ETL: cleaning, reshaping and routing events on their way into a warehouse or lakehouse
avoidWhen: An answer that’s an hour old is fine; a scheduled batch query is easier to write, test and rerun
Questions you can’t plan in advance; a stream job only answers the query it was started with
Each event just triggers one action, such as sending an email; a queue and workers are simpler
Nobody can look after it: long-running stateful jobs need checkpoints, upgrades and watching for lag and growing state
example: Card payments arrive on a `payments` topic, keyed by card number. A Flink job counts declined payments per card in one-minute tumbling windows by event time, with a watermark ten seconds behind the newest event so stragglers still count. More than five declines in a minute sends an alert. When a worker dies, the job restarts from its last checkpoint and rereads the topic from the offsets stored in it, so no decline is lost or counted twice.

providers.aws: Managed Service for Apache Flink (named Kinesis Data Analytics until 2023)
providers.oss: Apache Flink (StreamFusion, pre-1.0, runs Flink SQL natively in Rust), Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming, Arroyo; streaming databases and incremental views: Feldera (MIT core, paid Enterprise features), RisingWave (Apache 2.0; premium features need a licence key) and Materialize (BSL); ksqlDB (Confluent Community License); Redpanda Connect for stateless pipelines; Python: Quix Streams, Pathway (BSL), Bytewax (now community-maintained); Rust: Timely and Differential Dataflow, Streamling (FSL)

source: -- Flink SQL: page views per minute, by event time, waiting 5 s for stragglers
WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts - INTERVAL '5' SECOND
-- one row per page per window, emitted once the watermark passes window_end
SELECT window_start, window_end, page, COUNT(*) AS views
FROM TUMBLE(TABLE clicks, DESCRIPTOR(ts), INTERVAL '1' MINUTES)

diagram.caption: Clicks are split by user across two partitions, and each partition feeds one task of the job. Every event updates that task’s per-user state; only now and then does a window close and send a result on. All of each user’s events go to the same task, so its count lives in one place.

story: For years, “real time” meant queues and hand-written workers. At BackType, Nathan Marz recalled, most of that code dealt with moving and serialising messages rather than the actual logic, so he built Storm to hide the plumbing and released it in September 2011, after Twitter bought BackType. Exact results still came from batch jobs, so many teams ran the same logic twice: fast in a stream job, correct in Hadoop. In 2014 Jay Kreps called maintaining code for the same result in two distributed systems “exactly as painful as it seems like it would be”, and proposed replaying a retained log through the stream job instead.

Google’s MillWheel (2013) and Dataflow Model (2015) papers showed how a stream job could be correct on its own, with exactly-once state, event time, windows and watermarks. Apache Flink, which grew out of the Stratosphere research project and became a top-level Apache project in December 2014, paired those ideas with consistent snapshots of all its state. Kafka Streams (2016) put similar machinery into a library.

Today most engines also speak SQL, and the clouds sell them as services: Google’s Dataflow runs Apache Beam pipelines, Azure has Stream Analytics, and in 2023 AWS renamed Kinesis Data Analytics to Managed Service for Apache Flink, then retired its older SQL engine.

choices.why: Looking up a database for every event is slow and hammers the database. Keeping counts, windows and join buffers in local memory or RocksDB, split by key across tasks, keeps each step fast.

choices.choice: Event time and watermarks, not arrival time
choices.why: Events arrive late and out of order, and replays arrive all at once. Grouping by when things happened, and using watermarks to decide when a window is done, gives the same answer live and on replay.

choices.choice: Snapshot state and input positions together
choices.why: Writing every update somewhere durable would be too slow. Saving state and offsets as one consistent checkpoint lets a job rewind to that point after a crash, so nothing is lost or counted twice.

choices.choice: Replay instead of a second batch system
choices.why: If the input is kept in a log, fixing a bug means rerunning the stream job from the start, not keeping a separate batch pipeline in step with it.

timeline.text: Storm is open-sourced at Strange Loop, after Twitter buys BackType
Google’s MillWheel paper describes low watermarks and exactly-once processing
Flink becomes a top-level Apache project; Kreps questions the Lambda Architecture
The Dataflow Model paper sets out event time, windows and watermarks
Kafka Streams ships in Kafka 0.10; Spark 2.0 previews Structured Streaming
Kinesis Data Analytics becomes Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
AWS deletes the last Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL applications
